Selective Access to Tetrasubstituted Allenes

ABSTRACT: Metal hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)
has emerged as a powerful strategy for alkene hydrofunctionaliza-
tion, offering exceptional control over regio- and chemoselectivity.
However, conventional MHAT reactions with 1,3-enynes remain
limited to the 1,2-addition pathway. Herein, we report a
regioselective 1,4-hydroarylation of 1,3-enynes with various aryl
halides enabled by dual cobalt and nickel catalysis. This
transformation proceeds through cobalt(III)-H-mediated HAT to the 1,3-enynes, followed by nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling
with aryl halides, delivering a wide range of tetrasubstituted allenes in good to excellent yields. This work expands the scope of
Co(III)H-mediated radical hydrofunctionalization reactions and offers a modular strategy for constructing valuable, highly
substituted allene building blocks.
H
ydrofunctionalization of unsaturated hydrocarbons con-
stitutes one of the most crucial reactions in organic
synthesis, which allows for the conversion of simple olefins or
alkynes into more complex and diverse compounds, thus
facilitating the development of novel materials, pharmaceut-
icals, and various other valuable products.
1,2
In particular, the
first-row transition-metal (e.g., Fe, Mn and Co)-catalyzed
metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions
serve as a highly chemoselective means for Markovnikov
hydrofunctionalization of alkenes and have witnessed remark-
able progress.
3
Intermediate carbon-centered radicals derived
from MHAT exhibit versatile reactivity, with recent advances
highlighting their synthetic potential and mechanistic versa-
tility, including participation in classical radical transformations
(e.g., atom/group transfer and addition to unsaturated
bonds)
4,5
as well as subsequent oxidation or reduction to
enable radical-polar crossover processes (Scheme 1a).
6−8
However, in contrast to the well-developed hydrofunctional-
ization of simple styrene and unactivated alkenes, MHAT-
initiated hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes�versatile syn-
thons featuring both alkenyl and alkynyl moieties�remains
elusive and underexplored.
9
Such difficulty is unsurprising,
given the inherent challenges associated with the regiochemical
complexity, multiple possibilities, and potential overreactions
that exist as competing pathways that hinder the achievement
of high regioselectivity.
10
Seminal work by Carreira demon-
strated that cobalt(III)-hydride-initiated MHAT enables
selective hydrohydrazination of enynes, in which the propargyl
radical A generated in situ was directly addition to
azodicarboxylates, delivering a series of propargylic hydrazines
in useful yields (Scheme 1b).
9
Despite recently there have
been relevant attempts to test the feasibility of enyne in
MHAT reactions, successful functionalization has thus far been
confined to the 1,2-addition paradigm with alkynyl retention.
7c
In contrast, direct 1,4-hydrofunctionalization�a highly desir-
able route to synthetically valuable allene derivatives
11
remains
underexplored.
Recent works including our own have unveiled MHAT-
mediated hydrofunctionalizations of 1,3-dienes, in which a
regioselective 1,2- or 1,4-hydrofunctionalization can be
achieved through selective hydrogen-atom transfer from the
cobalt hydride species.
12
Inspired by these studies and due to
our continuous interest in Co(III)H-catalyzed radical reac-
tions,
8,12d
we questioned whether a propargylic radical could
be merged with Co(III)-H catalysis to enable 1,4-hydro-
arylation of enynes. We envisioned that MHAT from Co(III)-
H would initiate formation of propargyl radical/cobalt(II)
pairs, followed by isomerization to generate an allenylcobalt-
(III) intermediate C (Scheme 1a right), which can be
intercepted by catalytic organometal species such as catalytic
organonickel species, that would enable direct 1,4-hydro-
functionalization of 1,3-enynes to yield multisubstituted allenes
(Scheme 1b bottom). Successfully accomplishing this process
would expand the utilization of organocobalt to analogous
allenyl-Co(III) intermediates, significantly less explored in
cobalt-catalyzed MHAT transformation. Notably, the Shenvi
group creatively developed a Ni/Co(II)-catalyzed reductive
coupling hydroarylation of unactivated terminal alkenes

Herein, we reported the first investigation
of cobalt-hydride HAT initiated radical 1,4-hydroarylation of
1,3-enynes with aryl halides via dual Co/Ni catalysis (Scheme
1c). This reaction provides an efficient and straightforward
approach to synthesize valuable allenes featuring four different
functional group moieties in good to excellent yields.
We commenced this study by choosing 1-methoxy-4-(non-
2-en-4-yn-3-yl)benzene (1a) and p-trifluoromethyl iodoben-
zene (2a) as substrates. Pleasingly, under optimized conditions

reaction component (entries 2−4). Notably, no product was
observed in the absence of silanes, demonstrating their
essential function in facilitating Co(III)-mediated MHAT
reactions and potentially generating catalytically active Ni−H
species (entry 4). Based on the previous works reported by
Shenvi,
6a

combination with catalytic Co(II)Salen complex, which
effectively facilitates the conversion of Co(II) to Co(III) and
sustains the cobalt catalytic cycle,
7

product 3aa in 65% yield (entry 5). In comparison, the direct
use of the Co(III)Salen complex is more effective and can
avoid the requirement for stoichiometric oxidants. Other
silanes, such as TMDSO and PhSiH
3

facilitating the reaction, albeit with decreased yields (entries 6,
7). Switching the Co(III)-1 to its analogue Co(III)-3 or
Co(III)-4 also gave allene 3aa in 35−42% yield, but the
utilization of Co(III)-2 failed to deliver 3aa (entries 8, 9). The
use of other nickel catalysts and ligands in place of NiBr

With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we next
investigated the scope of allene synthesis with respect to the
substituents (R
1

substituent R
1
on the aryl moiety, the method was suitable for
installing various electron-donating and electron-withdrawing
substituents, including methoxy, alkyl, fluoro, chloro, and
trifluoromethyl, all of which were conveniently transformed to
the expected tetrasubstituted allene products 3bb−3kb in
good to excellent yields. The process was not detrimentally
influenced by the position (o-, m-, p-) of the substituent on the
phenyl ring; even ortho-substitution, which was regarded as
having a certain steric hindrance, can deliver the expected
products with outstanding yields. Similarly, the reaction of
disubstituted aryl (for 3lb−3nb) as well as electron-rich arene
(for 3ob) and naphthalene (for 3pa) substituted 1,3-enynes
also proceeded smoothly to afford allenes in good yields. In
addition, the present transformation was not disturbed by the
substituent R
2

a variety of enynes having an internal substituent R

terminal alkene moiety also performed well (see 3ub−3xb). As
for R

different lengths (for 3Ab−3Db), functionalized primary alkyl

groups (for 3Eb and 3Fb), and sterically bulkier cycloalkyl
groups (for 3Gc) and cyclohexenyl (3Hb) as well as ether
(3Ib) groups could be installed, delivering the corresponding
tetrasubstituted allenes in moderate to good yields. The tert-
butyl-substituted 1,3-enyne failed to yield 3Jb, likely due to
excessive steric hindrance.
The reaction scope was then extended to various aryl
electrophilic reagents (Scheme 3). A wide array of aryl iodides,
including those with electron-donating or electron-withdraw-
ing groups, underwent smooth coupling with 1,3-enyne to
deliver allene products 4a−4i in good to excellent yields.
Substrates with multiple fluorine substituents (4m, 4n),
heteroaryl iodides (4o, 4p), and diverse meta- or disubstituted
arenes including electron-deficient 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)-
iodobenzene (4j−4l, 4s−4w) all reacted smoothly to deliver
products in high yields. For broader synthetic interests, 4-CN-
and 4-COOMe-substituted iodobenzenes were also viable to
deliver the corresponding allene products 4q and 4r with yields
of 91% and 87%, respectively. In contrast, an alkyl iodide failed
to couple and led to only partial oxidation of 1,3-enyne.
Substrate evaluation beyond aryl iodides revealed that bromo
and chloro arenes were also viable coupling partners, affording
3aa in 65% and 37% yield, respectively, whereas aryl triflates
failed to react. Furthermore, the synthetic utility was
demonstrated on a 3.0 mmol scale, delivering 3aa in 80%
yield. Moreover, some bioactive molecules, such as cholesterol,
D -(−)-pantolactone, and structurally more complicated vitamin
E-derivated aryl iodides were conveniently transformed to the
corresponding allene products 4x−4z in good yields, which
demonstrated that this method would be suitable for late-stage
functionalization of complicated molecules.
A series of experiments were performed to probe the
reaction mechanism (Scheme 4). First, the introduction of a
stoichiometric amount of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl
(TEMPO) significantly attenuated the transformation, while
no TEMPO-trapped product 6 was detected (Scheme 4a). In
contrast, a “radical-clock” experiment with (2-
vinylcyclopropyl)benzene 7 led to ring-opened product 8 in
38% yield (Scheme 4b). In addition, diene 9 underwent
cyclization to give product 10 with 35% yield and 5:1 dr
(Scheme 4b). These phenomena reveal a radical mechanism,
which was further corroborated by the detection of a minor
coupling byproduct derived from propargyl radical and allenyl
radicals (see SI for details). A deuterium labeling experiment
using Ph
2
SiD
2
(>95% D) afforded d
1
-3cb with 0.95 D exclusive
incorporation at the alkene terminus, confirming the silane as
the hydrogen source and supporting a CoH-mediated MHAT
pathway (Scheme 4c).
To identify the active organometallic species in this cross-
coupling process, the isolable nickel(II) oxidative addition
intermediate 11 was synthesized (Scheme 4d) and evaluated in
control experiments.
14
When complex 11 was employed as the
nickel precatalyst in the reaction of 1,3-enyne (1c) with ethyl
4-iodobenzoate (2u) under standard conditions, allene 12 was
obtained in 58% yield (Scheme 4e, eq 1). In contrast, a
stoichiometric reaction of 11 with 1c in the absence of aryl
iodide afforded only trace amounts of 12 (<5% yield, eq 2).
Interestingly, when an additional 1.5 equiv of 4-chloroiodo-
benzene (2b) was employed as the coupling reagent, it was
found that the 4-chloroaryl-substituted allene 3cb was obtained
in 54% yield, but still with only 5% of product 12 originated
from the “precatalyst” 11 (Scheme 4e, eq 3). The low yield of
product 12 seems insufficient to support an arylnickel(II)
species as a feasible intermediate in the catalytic cycle, and the
mechanism that directs trapping of the propargyl/allenyl
radical derived from MHAT by an arylnickel(II) species to
form Ni(III) species followed by reductive elimination to form
coupled products can be excluded (the aryl iodide was not
consumed).
15
Meanwhile, in the absence of an oxidative agent,
the continuous production of Co−H is also halted.
Theoretically, at most, 10% of the C−C coupling products
will be formed. These results further encouraged us to consider
that Ni(II) complex 11 might transform into an active Ni
catalyst (e.g., Ni(I)) to prompt the reaction to occur.
Based upon collective mechanistic studies and previous
related literature,
6−17
a plausible reaction mechanism is
proposed in Scheme 5. The catalytic cycle begins with the in
situ formation of a cobalt hydride complex [Co(III)H] via
transmetalation of a SalenCo(III) catalyst with silane. Then, a
Co(III)H-mediated MHAT to the 1,3-enyne (1) generates the
propargyl radical A, which equilibrates with the allenyl radical
B and is trapped by Co(II) to form a metastable allenyl
cobalt(III) species C, more accurately described as an
equilibrium of a cage-pair.

active LNi(I) species, which undergoes oxidative addition with
aryl iodide 2 to afford LNi(III) intermediate D. Based on
recent work by Shenvi,
6a,13
a ligand transfer from allenyl
cobalt(III) C to the Ni(III) complex D is proposed to occur
via electron transfer/ligand transfer between the Co(III)/
Ni(III) organometallic pair within a solvent cage,
13
yielding
the key allenyl nickel(III) intermediate E and regenerating the
Co(III) catalyst. Finally, reductive elimination of the Ar−
Ni(III) E species delivers the C−C cross-coupling allene
products and regenerates Ni(I), thus closing the catalytic cycle.
Considering the isomerization between propargylic- and
allenyl-metal species, a possible reduction elimination pathway
originating from the propargylic-Ni(III)-Ar species E′ cannot
be ruled out at present.
■
CONCLUSION
In summary, we have developed an efficient MHAT-mediated
1,4-hydroarylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl halides via
synergistic cobalt/nickel catalysis. This MHAT-mediated
protocol provides direct access to diverse tetrasubstituted
allenes in high yields. These allene products serve as versatile
synthetic platforms for further elaboration through alkene
functionalization. This work expands the arsenal of MHAT
reactions by merging Co−H-mediated MHAT with Ni-
catalyzed cross-coupling, offering a novel strategy for allene
synthesis. Studies on the mechanism and development of
enantioselective variants are currently underway.

ABSTRACT: Metal hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)
has emerged as a powerful strategy for alkene hydrofunctionaliza-
tion, ofering exceptional control over regio- and chemoselectivity.
However, conventional MHAT reactions with 1,3-enynes remain
limited to the 1,2-addition pathway. Herein, we report a
regioselective 1,4-hydroarylation of 1,3-enynes with various aryl
halides enabled by dual cobalt and nickel catalysis. This

stitutes one of the most crucial reactions in organic
synthesis, which allows for the conversion of simple olefins or
alkynes into more complex and diverse compounds, thus
facilitating the development of novel materials, pharmaceut-
icals, and various other valuable products.<sup>1,2</sup> In particular, the
first-row transition-metal (e.g., Fe, Mn and Co)-catalyzed
metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions
serve as a highly chemoselective means for Markovnikov
hydrofunctionalization of alkenes and have witnessed remark-
able progress.<sup>3</sup> Intermediate carbon-centered radicals derived
from MHAT exhibit versatile reactivity, with recent advances
highlighting their synthetic potential and mechanistic versa-
tility, including participation in classical radical transformations
(e.g., atom/group transfer and addition to unsaturated
bonds)<sup>4,5</sup> as well as subsequent oxidation or reduction to
However, in contrast to the well-developed hydrofunctional
ization of simple styrene and unactivated alkenes, MHAT-
initiated hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes�versatile syn-
thons featuring both alkenyl and alkynyl moieties�remains
elusive and underexplored.<sup>9</sup> Such dificulty is unsurprising,
given the inherent challenges associated with the regiochemical
complexity, multiple possibilities, and potential overreactions
that exist as competing pathways that hinder the achievement
of high regioselectivity.<sup>10</sup> Seminal work by Carreira demon-
strated that cobalt(III)-hydride-initiated MHAT enables
selective hydrohydrazination of enynes, in which the propargyl
radical A generated in situ was directly addition to
azodicarboxylates, delivering a series of propargylic hydrazines
in useful yields (Scheme 1b).<sup>9</sup> Despite recently there have
been relevant attempts to test the feasibility of enyne in
MHAT reactions, successful functionalization has thus far been

confined to the 1,2-addition paradigm with alkynyl retention.<sup>7c</sup>
In contrast, direct 1,4-hydrofunctionalization�a highly desir-
able route to synthetically valuable allene derivatives<sup>11</sup> remains
underexplored.

Recent works including our own have unveiled MHAT-
mediated hydrofunctionalizations of 1,3-dienes, in which a
regioselective 1,2- or 1,4-hydrofunctionalization can be
achieved through selective hydrogen-atom transfer from the
cobalt hydride species.<sup>12</sup> Inspired by these studies and due to
our continuous interest in Co(III)H-catalyzed radical reac-
tions,<sup>8,12d</sup>
we questioned whether a propargylic radical could
be merged with Co(III)-H catalysis to enable 1,4-hydro-
arylation of enynes. We envisioned that MHAT from Co(III)-
H would initiate formation of propargyl radical/cobalt(II)
pairs, followed by isomerization to generate an allenylcobalt-
(III) intermediate C (Scheme 1a right), which can be
intercepted by catalytic organometal species such as catalytic
organonickel species, that would enable direct 1,4-hydro-
functionalization of 1,3-enynes to yield multisubstituted allenes
(Scheme 1b bottom). Successfully accomplishing this process
would expand the utilization of organocobalt to analogous
allenyl-Co(III) intermediates, significantly less explored in
cobalt-catalyzed MHAT transformation. Notably, the Shenvi
group creatively developed a Ni/Co(II)-catalyzed reductive
coupling hydroarylation of unactivated terminal alkenes

through an unprecedented radical alkyl-Co(III) to nickel direct
transmetalation.<sup>6a,13</sup> Herein, we reported the first investigation
of cobalt-hydride HAT initiated radical 1,4-hydroarylation of
1,3-enynes with aryl halides via dual Co/Ni catalysis (Scheme
1c). This reaction provides an eficient and straightforward
approach to synthesize valuable allenes featuring four diferent
functional group moieties in good to excellent yields.

■ CONCLUSION

In summary, we have developed an eficient MHAT-mediated
1,4-hydroarylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl halides via
synergistic cobalt/nickel catalysis. This MHAT-mediated
protocol provides direct access to diverse tetrasubstituted
allenes in high yields. These allene products serve as versatile
synthetic platforms for further elaboration through alkene
functionalization. This work expands the arsenal of MHAT
reactions by merging Co−H-mediated MHAT with Ni-
catalyzed cross-coupling, ofering a novel strategy for allene
synthesis. Studies on the mechanism and development of
enantioselective variants are currently underway.
